Test each feature group for a difference between two levels

Source: R/cellpaintr.R
calculateStats.Rd

Average the leave-one-out prediction scores of predictLOO per patient and level, and test in each feature group whether the interest level has higher scores than the reference level.

Usage

calculateStats(
  sce,
  target,
  group,
  assay_type = "tfmfeatures",
  method = c("permutation", "corrected", "nadeau_bengio", "t"),
  n_permutations = 999
)

Arguments

sce

Output of predictLOO

target

character(1), name of the column of colData(sce) with the condition of each cell, such as the drug

group

character(1), name of the column of colData(sce) with the replicate of each cell, such as the patient; the replicates are the folds of the leave-one-out cross-validation

assay_type

character(1), name of the assay with the features

method

Either `"permutation"` (default) for a permutation test that relabels whole patients, `"corrected"` for the corrected paired t-test, `"nadeau_bengio"` for the paired t-test with the correction of Nadeau and Bengio, or `"t"` for p-values from the t-distribution

n_permutations

Largest number of relabelings besides the observed labels; if there are more, this many are drawn at random

Value

data.frame with one row per feature group and the columns `Target` (interest level), `Feature` (feature group), `pvalue`, and `log2FoldChange` (log2 ratio of the mean scores of the interest and the reference level). With the permutation test, the attribute `relabelings` holds the number of relabelings, the observed one included.

Details

The test statistic is the one-sided t-statistic for higher mean scores in the interest level. It is paired if every patient (`group`) has cells of both levels, and uses a pooled variance otherwise.

With `method = "permutation"` (the default), the p-value comes from relabeling whole patients: in a paired design, the two levels of a patient are swapped; in an unpaired design, the levels are permuted across patients; and in a mixed design, where only some patients have cells of both levels, the levels of those patients are swapped and the levels of the other patients are permuted among them. For each relabeling, all leave-one-out models are refitted with the settings of the call to predictLOO, and the p-value is the proportion of relabelings, the observed one included, with a statistic at least as large. Exchanging the two levels in all patients at once turns every score into one minus the score and leaves the statistic unchanged, so relabelings come in pairs with the same statistic. Whenever this exchange is itself a relabeling (always in a paired design, and if the patients with one level are split evenly between the two levels otherwise), one patient keeps its labels, which halves the number of relabelings and refits without changing the test. If there are at most `n_permutations + 1` relabelings (\(2^{n-1}\) for \(n\) patients in a paired design), all of them are enumerated and the test is exact; otherwise, `n_permutations` relabelings are drawn at random. The smallest attainable p-value is one over the number of relabelings, \(2^{1-n}\) in a paired design. Because all models are refitted for every relabeling, the test takes that many times longer than predictLOO. Use set.seed for reproducible results.

With `method = "corrected"`, the p-value comes from a corrected paired t-test, which needs a paired design with at least three patients. Each patient is in the training set of every other patient's model, which makes the score differences of different patients positively correlated, so the t-statistic is too large. If each score difference is a sum of pairwise interactions with the other patients, two score differences have correlation \(1/(n-1)\) for \(n\) patients, and the t-statistic is too large by the factor \(\sqrt{2(n-1)/(n-2)}\). The corrected t-test divides the t-statistic by this factor and refers it to the t-distribution with \(n-1\) degrees of freedom. It needs no refits, and its p-values are not limited to multiples of \(2^{1-n}\), but it is approximate.

With `method = "nadeau_bengio"`, the t-statistic is divided instead by \(\sqrt{(2n-1)/(n-1)}\), the factor of the corrected resampled t-test of Nadeau and Bengio (2003, Machine Learning 52:239-281) for \(n\) splits with one held-out patient each, which assumes a correlation of \(1/n\) instead of \(1/(n-1)\). It corrects less and therefore has more power, which pays off if part of each score difference is independent of the other patients, for example noise from the random seeds of the forests. If the score differences consist mostly of pairwise interactions, it can exceed the nominal level with four to six patients, where `method = "corrected"` holds it. It needs a paired design with at least two patients and no refits.

With `method = "t"`, the p-value comes from the t-distribution. This is fast but anti-conservative, because the score differences of different patients are positively correlated.

Examples

set.seed(23)
cell_file <- generateData()
sce <- loadData(cell_file)
sce <- transformScale(sce)

sce$Drug <- as.factor(sce$Drug)
sce$Drug <- relevel(sce$Drug, ref = "D1")

sce_single <- predictLOO(
    sce,
    target = "Drug", group = "Patient",
    interest_level = "D7", reference_level = "D1",
    n_threads = 1
)

# permutation test; by default, it enumerates all 64 relabelings of the
# six patients, here 9 random relabelings keep the example fast
calculateStats(sce_single,
    target = "Drug", group = "Patient",
    n_permutations = 9
)
#> Permutation test with 10 relabelings of 6 levels of 'Patient' (paired design); smallest attainable p-value 1/10.
#> 'P1' keeps its labels, because exchanging the two levels of 'Drug' in all levels of 'Patient' at once gives the same statistic.
#>   Target Feature pvalue log2FoldChange
#> 1     D7     all    0.1      0.9328005

# corrected t-test: no refits
calculateStats(sce_single,
    target = "Drug", group = "Patient",
    method = "corrected"
)
#>   Target Feature       pvalue log2FoldChange
#> 1     D7     all 0.0001791293      0.9328005

# correction of Nadeau and Bengio: no refits, corrects less
calculateStats(sce_single,
    target = "Drug", group = "Patient",
    method = "nadeau_bengio"
)
#>   Target Feature       pvalue log2FoldChange
#> 1     D7     all 0.0001322961      0.9328005

# p-values from the t-distribution: fast but anti-conservative
calculateStats(sce_single,
    target = "Drug", group = "Patient",
    method = "t"
)
#>   Target Feature       pvalue log2FoldChange
#> 1     D7     all 1.971207e-05      0.9328005
